THE ANCIENT COVENANT RECORD

New Jerusalem — 4Q554-555, 11Q18

YERUSHALAYIM HADASHAH

The New Jerusalem — Complete

4Q554, 4Q555, 11Q18, 1Q32, 2Q24, 5Q15 — All Fragments

Eschatological Vision — Measured City — Temple Dimensions — Gates of the Tribes

PRIMARY MANUSCRIPT AUTHORITIES

4Q554 — Cave 4, Qumran — Aramaic — Largest witness — Primary authority

4Q555 — Cave 4, Qumran — Aramaic — Parallel fragments

11Q18 — Cave 11, Qumran — Aramaic — Well-preserved columns

Additional fragments: 1Q32, 2Q24, 5Q15 — Minor witnesses

Qumran Aramaic composition — No Christian contamination — Pre-1st century BCE

COMPARATIVE NOTES AT END OF EVERY CHAPTER

DSS · ORIT GE'EZ · MASORETIC VARIANT · CRITICAL NOTE

YHWH / 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 and The Creator only — no substitute titles

INTRODUCTION TO THE NEW JERUSALEM TEXT

1 The New Jerusalem text is a Qumran Aramaic composition presenting an angelic tour of an eschatological city — a future Jerusalem of perfect dimensions, proper temple, and righteous governance. It is attested across six manuscript witnesses from five different caves, making it one of the most widely circulated non-biblical texts in the Qumran corpus.

2 The text follows the literary form of the guided visionary tour, in which the seer is led by an angelic figure who measures and explains the dimensions of the holy city. This form is ancient in the Afro-Asiatic tradition, appearing in the later chapters of Yehezkel and developed here into a full independent composition.

3 The New Jerusalem text predates the Christian book of Revelation by at least two centuries. The appearance of similar imagery in Revelation reflects borrowing from this ancient Qumran tradition, not the reverse. Western scholarship has consistently inverted this relationship, treating Revelation as the original and the Qumran text as parallel rather than source.

COMPARATIVE MANUSCRIPT NOTES

[DSS] The New Jerusalem text was published in the DJD series across multiple volumes due to the distribution of fragments across different caves. The Aramaic language, the angelic guide format, and the detailed metrological system all confirm a Qumran composition of the 2nd to 1st century BCE. No later addition or Christian interpolation has been identified in any fragment.

[ORIT GE'EZ] The Orit Ge'ez tradition does not contain a direct parallel to the New Jerusalem text. However the concept of a heavenly city whose earthly form will be revealed at the end of days is consistent with the eschatological framework of both the Ge'ez Chanokh (chapters 24-26) and the Ge'ez Yovelim. The heavenly prototype of earthly sacred space is an ancient Afro-Asiatic theological concept.

[MASORETIC VARIANT] Yehezkel chapters 40-48 in the Masoretic text presents a detailed temple vision with angelic guide and precise measurements. The New Jerusalem text develops this tradition into a full city vision. The Masoretic Yehezkel is the closest canonical parallel but the New Jerusalem text is more expansive and eschatologically explicit.

[CRITICAL NOTE] The New Jerusalem text has been appropriated by Christian scholarship as a precursor to Revelation and by some modern movements as a literal blueprint for physical rebuilding. Both appropriations fundamentally misread the text. The Qumran community understood the New Jerusalem as an eschatological reality — the form of the age to come — not a construction plan and not a Christian theological symbol.

THE VISION OF THE NEW JERUSALEM

COLUMN 1 — THE ANGELIC GUIDE AND THE FIRST MEASUREMENTS — 4Q554 Fragment 1

1 [And the man led me into the city and measured the wall of the city with a measuring reed]. The wall was built of pure stone and its height was immense. The gate of the wall opened toward the east and toward the west and toward the north and toward the south.

2 And he measured the street of the city: the width of the street was twelve reeds and the length of the street from the eastern gate to the western gate was thirty stadia. And the streets were paved with white stone and black stone alternating.

3 On each side of every street were houses built of pure stone, each house joined to the next, each door of cedar wood and the lintels of pure gold. And before each house was a garden planted with trees and the trees bore fruit according to their kind.

4 And I asked the angel: who shall dwell in these houses? And he said: the righteous ones of Yisra'el who have walked in the mystery of existence and kept the covenant of YHWH. Their names are written in the book of life and these are their eternal dwellings.

5 And he measured the blocks of the city: each block was a perfect square of reeds. And in each block were four houses. And between the blocks ran the streets, ordered according to the four directions of the heavens, so that the whole city was a single ordered pattern.

6 Then he showed me the central street that ran from the main gate to the temple mount. It was wider than all the others and paved with pure white stone. No unclean thing had ever walked on it and no unclean thing ever would.

COMPARATIVE MANUSCRIPT NOTES

[DSS] 4Q554 Fragment 1 is the primary witness for the opening measurement sequence. The reed measurements in this text are consistent with the sacred cubit system used in the Temple Scroll and in the Yehezkel vision, confirming that the New Jerusalem text belongs to the same Qumran priestly-eschatological tradition.

[ORIT GE'EZ] The Orit Ge'ez tradition in Chanokh 24-26 describes a guided tour of the eschatological mountain and the tree of life at its center. The New Jerusalem text develops this into an urban eschatological vision. Both texts belong to the ancient Afro-Asiatic tradition of heavenly archetypes that are revealed to the righteous as the destination of the covenant community.

[MASORETIC VARIANT] Yehezkel 40-48 contains the closest Masoretic parallel. The New Jerusalem text uses a similar measurement system and angelic guide format but expands from temple to full city. The relationship between the two texts confirms that the New Jerusalem tradition developed from the Yehezkel vision, not independently. The DSS text represents a further development of the prophetic tradition.

[CRITICAL NOTE] The description of the righteous inhabitants as those who walked in the mystery of existence confirms that the New Jerusalem text belongs within the 4QInstruction theological framework: the raz nihyeh is not merely an intellectual concept but the ethical path whose end is the eschatological city. This integration of wisdom and eschatology is characteristic of the most theologically sophisticated Qumran compositions.

COLUMN 2 — THE GATES OF THE TWELVE TRIBES — 11Q18 Columns 1-3

1 And he showed me the twelve gates of the city, three on each side according to the four directions. Each gate was named for one of the sons of Yaakov. The gates on the east were for Re'uven and Yehudah and Levi. The gates on the north were for Yosef and Binyamin and Dan.

2 The gates on the west were for Shim'on and Yissakhar and Zevulun. The gates on the south were for Gad and Asher and Naftali. Each gate was of pure stone and the name of the tribe was inscribed above it in letters of gold.

3 And the width of each gate was two reeds and the height was three reeds. And the gate posts were of cedar and the doors were of pure gold that shone like the sun when the light fell upon them.

4 Before each gate stood two pillars of white stone and upon each pillar were inscribed the blessings of the tribe whose name was on the gate. The blessing of Moshe from Devarim and the blessing of Yaakov from Bereshit were both written there.

5 And I saw that there was no darkness in the city. The glory of YHWH illuminated it and there was no need for sun or moon within its walls. The light came from the presence of The Creator and it was constant and without shadow.

6 And the angel said to me: write what you have seen. For these things will come to pass at the appointed time. What YHWH has measured in the heavens will be established on the earth. His word does not return to Him without accomplishing its purpose.

COMPARATIVE MANUSCRIPT NOTES

[DSS] 11Q18 Columns 1-3 contain the gate sequence with tribal names, which is well-preserved in the Cave 11 manuscript. The assignment of specific gates to specific tribes establishes a geography of restored tribal identity in the eschatological city. This confirms that the New Jerusalem vision is about the restoration of the complete twelve-tribe covenant community.

[ORIT GE'EZ] The twelve tribes receiving named gates in the eschatological city parallels the Yovelim framework in the Orit Ge'ez which carefully tracks the tribal allocations and boundaries as part of the divine ordering of Yisra'el. The tribal framework is fundamental to the Afro-Asiatic covenantal vision of the restored community.

[MASORETIC VARIANT] Yehezkel 48:30-35 in the Masoretic text also assigns named gates to the twelve tribes. The New Jerusalem text develops this tradition with greater architectural detail and embeds it within the full measurement of the city rather than presenting it as a concluding note. The Masoretic version is a condensed form of what the New Jerusalem text presents in full.

[CRITICAL NOTE] The absence of darkness and the light emanating from the divine presence rather than from sun or moon is a direct assertion that in the eschatological city the mediation of natural light — which in ancient Afro-Asiatic cosmology was associated with divine beings such as the sun deity — is replaced by the unmediated presence of YHWH. This is a theological statement of pure monotheism: no intermediate divine powers, only The Creator.
